summary: Vitamin D (cholecalciferol/D3 from skin and animal sources, ergocalciferol/D2 from plants) is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization. It is hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and then in the kidney to the active hormone calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. It is used to prevent and treat deficiency, rickets, and osteomalacia and as an adjunct in osteoporosis. Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia/bone pain in adults; excessive intake causes hypercalcemia with nausea, weakness, and renal impairment. This is a supplement/group entry covering both common forms.

moa: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid that functions as a prohormone. After ingestion or cutaneous synthesis it is hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcifediol) and then in the kidney by 1-alpha-hydroxylase to the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor to increase intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, promotes renal reabsorption of calcium, and works with parathyroid hormone to mobilize calcium from bone and support normal bone mineralization. Through these actions it maintains serum calcium and phosphate within the range needed for normal neuromuscular function and bone formation.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to vitamin D or formulation components
Malabsorption-related decision aside, evidence of vitamin D toxicity
relative: Hypercalciuria or history of calcium-containing renal stones
Severe renal impairment (use active analogues; monitor closely)
Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease (increased sensitivity to vitamin D)
Concurrent thiazide diuretics or high-dose calcium

preg: At recommended dietary intakes (RDA 600 IU/day) vitamin D is required and considered safe in pregnancy. High doses can cause hypercalcemia, which may be harmful to the fetus; use high-dose therapy only under medical supervision.
lact: Vitamin D requirements (RDA 600 IU/day) are met safely during lactation. Only small amounts pass into breast milk, so exclusively breastfed infants typically need their own vitamin D supplementation (about 400 IU/day).
renal: In moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation is impaired, so ordinary vitamin D may not be activated adequately; active forms such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol are usually required. Monitor serum calcium and phosphate carefully because of the risk of hypercalcemia and metastatic calcification.
hepatic: Severe hepatic disease can impair the 25-hydroxylation step and the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; monitor 25-hydroxyvitamin D response and adjust the dose accordingly.

major: Thiazide diuretics with high vitamin D/calcium intake - increased risk of hypercalcemia
moderate: Digoxin - hypercalcemia from vitamin D excess can precipitate digoxin toxicity/arrhythmias
Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine) - increase vitamin D catabolism, raising requirements
Glucocorticoids - reduce vitamin D-mediated calcium absorption
Orlistat, cholestyramine, mineral oil - reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamin D
minor: Magnesium-containing antacids - risk of hypermagnesemia in renal failure with high-dose vitamin D
interactions.food: Absorbed better when taken with a fat-containing meal.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; chronic heavy alcohol use can impair vitamin D status.
interactions.diagnostics: Status is assessed by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D; excess causes hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.

common: Generally well tolerated at recommended doses (few or no effects)
emergency: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, acute kidney injury)

monitoring: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D to assess status and guide dosing
Serum calcium and phosphate (especially with high doses)

missed: If you miss a daily dose, take it when you remember the same day; if it is nearly the next day, skip it and resume your schedule. For weekly high-dose regimens, take the missed dose as soon as you remember and then continue weekly. Do not double up.
overdose: Excessive vitamin D causes hypervitaminosis D with hypercalcemia: nausea, vomiting, weakness, constipation, polyuria, dehydration, confusion, and, with chronic excess, renal impairment and soft-tissue calcification. Management is to stop vitamin D and calcium, give fluids, and treat hypercalcemia (loop diuretics, corticosteroids, and in severe cases calcitonin or bisphosphonates) with monitoring of serum calcium and renal function.
